key: THE rich new car hath been equipped at morning; four yokes it hath, three whips, seven reins to guide it: Ten-sided, friendly to mankind, light-winner, that must be urged to speed with prayers and wishes.
s: Opening a hymn that calls Indra to the Soma with ever more horses, the verse pictures a car; Sāyaṇa, on 2.18.1, first reads the car as the morning sacrifice, its yokes the pressing-stones, its whips three pitches of voice, its reins the seven metres.
src: Sāyaṇa, Vedārthaprakāśa, on Rig Veda 2.18.1, sa.wikisource (printed edition not named), revision 208756 (2019)

opened.locator: 2.18.1 and its note on ratha as yajna

evidence.words: रथः रंहणाद्रथो यज्ञः । स च नवः । नूयते स्तूयतेऽत्रेति नवः स्तुतिमान् । सस्निः ॥ ‘स्ना शौचे'। ‘आदृगमहन’’ इति किन्प्रत्ययः । शुद्धः । एवंविधो यज्ञः प्रातः प्रातःकाले योजि अयोज्यस्माभिः । चतुर्युगः । युज्यन्त इति युगानि ग्रावाणः । चत्वारि युगानि यस्य स तथोक्तः । अध्वर्य्वाद्यृत्विगभिप्रायं वा । त्रिकशः । तिस्रः कशा वाचो मन्द्रमध्यमोत्कृष्टरूपो यस्य स तथोक्तः । सवनत्रयाभिप्रायं वा । सप्तरश्मिः । अश्नुवते व्याप्नुवन्ति कर्माणीति रश्मयश्छन्दांसि । सप्तसंख्याकानि गायत्र्यादीनि छन्दांसि यस्य स तथोक्तः ।
evidence.gloss: Ratha, the car, named from raṃhaṇa (speeding), is the sacrifice. It is nava, praiseworthy, and sasni, pure. Such a sacrifice was yoked by us at morning time. Four-yoked: yokes, so called because they are joined, are the pressing-stones; or it refers to the adhvaryu and the other priests. Three-whipped: whose three whips are speech in its low, middle and high forms; or it refers to the three pressings. Seven-reined: reins, so called because they pervade the rites, are the metres; it has seven metres, the gāyatrī and the rest.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 2.18.1, at [208,1]). Opened the packet for 2.18.1: Sāyaṇa glosses ratha as yajña yoked at morning (prātaḥkāle ayoji), the four yokes as the pressing-stones (grāvāṇaḥ), the three whips as speech in low, middle and high tones, the seven reins as the seven metres beginning with gāyatrī, then gives a second reading (yadvā) as Indra’s chariot yoked with horses at the morning pressing, which the sentence’s ‘first reads’ honours. Wilson translates the verse as a sacrifice and his note gives the same derivation. Plain sense matches the hymn (Indra summoned with 2 up to 100 horses, 2.18.4 to 6) and repeats no four words of the key. Revision 208756 dated 2019-08-04 by the Wikisource API. entry-check ok.
